{{Short description|Equation of state in cosmology}}
{{cosmology}}
In [[physical cosmology|cosmology]], the '''equation of state''' of a [[perfect fluid]] is characterized by a [[dimensionless]] number <math>w</math>, equal to the ratio of its [[pressure]] <math>p </math> to its [[energy density]] <math>\varepsilon</math>: 
<math display="block">w \equiv \frac{p}{\varepsilon}.</math>
It is closely related to the thermodynamic [[equation of state]] and [[ideal gas law]].

==The equation==
The [[perfect gas]] equation of state may be written as 
<math display="block">p = \rho RT = \rho c_s^2</math>
where <math> \rho</math> is the mass density, <math>R</math> is the particular gas constant, <math>T</math> is the temperature and <math>c_s=\sqrt{RT}</math> is a characteristic thermal speed of the molecules. Thus
<math display="block">w \equiv \frac{p}{\rho c^2} =  \frac{\rho c_s^2}{\rho c^2} = \frac{c_s^2}{c^2}\approx 0</math>
where <math>c</math> is the speed of light, <math>\varepsilon = \rho c^2</math> and <math>c_s\ll c</math> for a "cold" gas.

===FLRW equations and the equation of state===
The equation of state may be used in [[Friedmann–Lemaître–Robertson–Walker]] (FLRW) equations to describe the evolution of an isotropic universe filled with a perfect fluid. If <math>a</math> is the [[Scale factor (cosmology)|scale factor]] then 
<math display="block">\varepsilon \propto a^{-3(1+w)}.</math>
If the fluid is the dominant form of matter in a [[Shape of the universe#Flat universe|flat universe]], then
<math display="block">a \propto t^{\frac{2}{3(1+w)}},</math>
where <math>t</math> is the proper time.

In general the [[Friedmann equations|Friedmann acceleration equation]] is
<math display="block">3 \frac{\ddot{a}}{a} = \Lambda - 4 \pi G \left(\varepsilon + 3p\right)</math>
where <math> \Lambda</math> is the [[cosmological constant]] and <math>G</math> is [[Newton's constant]], and <math>\ddot{a}</math> is the second [[proper time]] derivative of the scale factor.

If we define (what might be called "effective") energy density and pressure as
<math display="block">\begin{align}
\varepsilon' &\equiv \varepsilon + \frac{\Lambda}{8 \pi G} \\[1ex]
p' &\equiv p - \frac{\Lambda}{8 \pi G}
\end{align}</math>
and <math display="block"> p' = w'\varepsilon'</math>
the acceleration equation may be written as
<math display="block">\frac{\ddot a}{a}=-\frac{4}{3}\pi G\left(\varepsilon' + 3p'\right) = -\frac{4}{3} \pi G \left(1+3w'\right)\varepsilon'</math>

===Non-relativistic particles===
The equation of state for ordinary non-[[theory of relativity|relativistic]] 'matter' (e.g. cold dust) is <math>w = 0</math>, which means that its energy density decreases as <math>\varepsilon \propto a^{-3} = V^{-1}</math>, where <math>V</math> is a volume. In an expanding universe, the total energy of non-relativistic matter remains constant, with its density decreasing as the volume increases.

===Radiation-dominated ultra-relativistic case===
The equation of state for ultra-relativistic 'radiation' (including [[neutrino]]s, and in the very early universe other particles that later became non-relativistic) is <math>w = 1/3</math> which means that its energy density decreases as <math>\varepsilon \propto a^{-4}</math>. In an expanding universe, the energy density of radiation decreases more quickly than the volume expansion, because its wavelength is [[red-shift]]ed.

===Stiff matter===
Stiff matter is governed by the [[Zeldovich equation of state]] with <math>w = 1</math> which means that its energy density decreases as <math>\varepsilon \propto a^{-6}</math>.

===Acceleration of cosmic inflation===
[[Cosmic inflation]] and the  [[Accelerating universe|accelerated expansion]] of the universe can be characterized by the equation of state of [[dark energy]]. In the simplest case, the equation of state of the [[cosmological constant]] is <math>w = -1</math>. In this case, the above expression for the scale factor is not valid and <math>a\propto e^{Ht}</math>, where the constant {{math|''H''}} is the [[Hubble parameter]]. More generally, the expansion of the universe is accelerating for any equation of state <math>w < -1/3</math>. The accelerated expansion of the Universe was indeed observed.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Hogan |first=Jenny |date=2007-07-01 |title=Welcome to the dark side |url=https://www.nature.com/articles/448240a |journal=Nature |language=en |volume=448 |issue=7151 |pages=240–245 |doi=10.1038/448240a |pmid=17637630 |issn=1476-4687|url-access=subscription }}</ref> The observed value of equation of state of cosmological constant is near {{formatnum:-1}} from three different major studies.<ref>{{Cite journal |last=Ludwick |first=Kevin J. |date=2017-09-14 |title=The viability of phantom dark energy: A review |url=https://www.worldscientific.com/doi/abs/10.1142/S0217732317300257 |journal=Modern Physics Letters A |volume=32 |issue=28 |pages=1730025 |doi=10.1142/S0217732317300257 |issn=0217-7323|arxiv=1708.06981 |bibcode=2017MPLA...3230025L }}</ref>

Hypothetical [[phantom dark energy]] would have an equation of state <math>w < -1</math>, and would cause a [[Big Rip]]. Using the existing data, it is still impossible to distinguish between phantom <math>w < -1 </math> and non-phantom <math>w \ge -1 </math>.

===Fluids===
In an expanding universe, fluids with larger equations of state disappear more quickly than those with smaller equations of state. This is the origin of the [[flatness problem|flatness]] and [[monopole problem|monopole]] problems of the [[Big Bang]]: [[curvature]] has <math>w = -1/3</math> and monopoles have <math>w = 0</math>, so if they were around at the time of the early Big Bang, they should still be visible today. These problems are solved by cosmic inflation which has <math>w \approx -1</math>. Measuring the equation of state of dark energy is one of the largest efforts of [[observational cosmology]]. By accurately measuring <math>w</math>, it is hoped that the cosmological constant could be distinguished from [[quintessence (physics)|quintessence]] which has <math>w \ne -1</math>.

===Scalar modeling===
A [[scalar field]] <math> \phi</math> can be viewed as a sort of perfect fluid with equation of state
<math display="block">w = \frac{\frac{1}{2}\dot{\phi}^2-V(\phi)}{\frac{1}{2}\dot{\phi}^2+V(\phi)},</math>
where <math> \dot{\phi}</math> is the time-derivative of <math> \phi</math> and <math>V(\phi)</math> is the potential energy. A free (<math>V = 0</math>) scalar field has <math>w = 1</math>, and one with vanishing kinetic energy is equivalent to a cosmological constant: <math>w = -1</math>. Any equation of state in between, but not crossing the <math>w = -1</math> barrier known as the Phantom Divide Line (PDL),<ref>{{cite journal
| first     = Alexander
| date      = 2005
| title     = Can dark energy evolve to the Phantom?
| journal   = Phys. Rev. D
| article-number     = 023515
| last      = Vikman
| volume    = 71
| issue     = 2
| doi       = 10.1103/PhysRevD.71.023515
| arxiv     = astro-ph/0407107 
|bibcode = 2005PhRvD..71b3515V | s2cid = 119013108
}}</ref> is achievable, which makes scalar fields useful models for many phenomena in cosmology.
